summary:
Argentina's Gender Identity Law 26,743 was approved by the Chamber of Deputies by 167 votes to 17 with 7 abstentions and by the Senate on 9 May 2012, and promulgated on 24 May 2012. It allows adults to change legal gender, image and birth name on civil registries without surgery, hormone therapy, a psychiatric diagnosis labelling abnormality, or approval by a doctor or judge. The United Nations described the statute as a pioneering step for transgender rights in the region.

On 20 July 2021, Decree 476/2021 required the national civil registry, RENAPER, to offer a third gender marker X on all national identity cards and passports, including for non-citizen permanent residents who hold Argentine identity cards. Mendoza Province and Santa Fe Province had earlier allowed applicants to leave the sex entry blank.

The 2012 law also grants adults access to sex reassignment surgery and hormone therapy through public and private health care plans, with equal health care access for non-binary, transgender or gender non-conforming people. Since 2010 no mental-health diagnosis may be made exclusively on the basis of sexual choice or identity. A 2007 Supreme Court ruling recognised a 17-year-old's right to undergo the sex-change process and change documents; Marcela Romero won legal identity change in 2009, and in October 2013 a six-year-old designated male at birth became the first transgender child to have her name officially changed without a judicial process.

In February 2025 the government issued a decree banning gender-affirming surgery and hormone therapy for people under 18, alongside a second decree on the housing of transgender people in prisons. Legal experts described the decrees as illegal and unconstitutional. In April 2025 a Federal Court ruled the care ban unconstitutional and restored access nationwide.

Penal Code Article 80(4), amended in 2012, imposes life imprisonment for a killing motivated by hatred based on gender identity or expression. The aggravating circumstance for a gender-motivated killing is not currently applied: on 5 April 2025 the Supreme Court left standing the life sentence of Gabriel Marino for the 2015 murder of trans activist Diana Sacayán but rejected attempts to reinstate the travesticidio aggravator that a cassation court had removed in 2020.

As of 2019 no national law expressly dealt with discrimination or harassment on the basis of gender identity or sexual orientation; only Buenos Aires city and Rosario provided local coverage, and a 2010 amendment approved by the Chamber of Deputies was never voted by the Senate. The national anti-discrimination agency was abolished and shut down in February 2024. Discrimination against National Public Administration employees on the basis of sexual orientation has been illegal since 2006.

The Observatorio Nacional de Crímenes de Odio recorded at least 227 hate crimes based on sexual orientation or gender identity in 2025, a record year averaging one every 38 hours. The figure is a raw count that aggregates sexual orientation and gender identity and is not disaggregated by victim group; no population denominator is provided, so it cannot be read as a per-capita magnitude or as a trans-specific rate.

Trans activists interviewed in Buenos Aires on 4 April 2025, among them figures from organisations named for Diana Sacayán and Lohana Berkins, said the Milei government's policies had made the community more vulnerable to violence and described the situation as chaotic and desperate. Outright International's current country assessment records negative ratings on gender recognition, same-sex relations and organisation registration, and an overall deterioration.

Marriage for same-sex couples has been legal since 15 July 2010, the first such law in Latin America, carrying the same benefits and protections as opposite-sex couples, including adoption since July 2010. Nationwide unión convivencial took effect on 1 August 2015, after earlier civil-union schemes endorsed in Buenos Aires city and Río Negro Province in 2002-2003 and in Villa Carlos Paz in 2007 and Río Cuarto in 2009 without adoption. A trans visitor in what would be locally classed as a same-sex relationship has the same route to legal recognition as other couples.
tangentialFactors:
State persecution of LGBT people under the dictatorship included murder, beating, rape and disappearance, with those targeted treated as disordered, decadent and sub-human. Specific episodes recorded include the 1978 World Cup cleansing arrests and beatings, and the murder of 18 gay men, among them an FLH activist, by Comando Condor between January 1982 and January 1983. In 2023, trans women survivors testified in court that they were held in dictatorship-era secret prisons where they were hunted by the state and, once imprisoned, forced to perform sexual acts in exchange for food.

Argentina was the first Latin American country to legalise marriage equality, in 2010, and passed one of the world's most progressive gender identity laws in 2012. The World Health Organization cited Argentina in 2015 as an exemplary country for providing transgender rights, and BBC Mundo assessed in 2014 that Argentina led the trans revolution in the world, tying that judgement to the law, alternative schools and the first transgender community centre rather than to tolerance polling.

Military reform passed on 27 February 2009 and took effect six months later, allowing gay, lesbian and bisexual service and banning sexual-orientation discrimination in the armed forces. The ban on gay and bisexual men donating blood was abolished in September 2015.

Reports of bullying against LGBT people, especially young people, remain common, and sex education under the 2006 law is criticised for insufficient prevention of LGBT bullying. In 2015 a judge reduced the sentence for the rape of a six-year-old boy on the basis of the child's homosexual orientation, a decision condemned as a disgrace.
localsOnly:
Formal employment exclusion persists, with most trans women limited to sex work. Reported life expectancy for trans people is 35 years, and 5 in 10 trans men report suicidal ideation with 4 in 10 reporting attempts. Family expulsion and hostile treatment are reported particularly in the more socially conservative provinces.

Conditions in custody and health settings shifted after the 2012 law: physical mistreatment of detained trans women fell from 48.3 per cent to under 10 per cent and sexual abuse from 43 per cent to under 10 per cent; avoidance of health centres for fear of discrimination fell from nearly half to 5.3 per cent, with hospital placement by affirmed gender and name. In 2005 a judge ordered Córdoba prison authorities to allow conjugal visits between gay prisoners and their partners.

Trans community infrastructure includes a publicly funded Casa Trans scheduled to open in December 2014 in Caballito, Buenos Aires, the Mocha Celis school in Chacarita serving as an educational refuge, and a proposed tax exemption for firms hiring trans workers. By May 2014 over half of the trans population had updated their DNI.

On parenting, a 2013 law approved 204 to 1 with 10 abstentions gave lesbian couples equal access to IVF, and Article 562 provides for filiation by procreative will. In 2024 the Supreme Court rejected a gay couple's surrogacy claim seeking a new birth certificate omitting the surrogate woman.
outOfScopeNotes:
The 2025 hate-crime total aggregates sexual orientation and gender identity and is not broken down by victim group; the sources provide no general homicide rate against which any trans-specific rate could be compared, so no severity comparison can be made from this figure.

Attitudinal polling cited for Argentina concerns homosexuality rather than transgender people: about 76 per cent acceptance in a 2020 Pew poll, highest in South America; 74 per cent in a 2013 poll rising to 81 per cent among younger respondents; two-thirds favouring same-sex marriage in a 2009 survey; and 75 per cent supporting marriage in an early 2007 Buenos Aires poll. No transgender-specific public-attitude polling was identified.

The April 2025 Federal Court ruling restored gender-affirming care access nationwide, but the sources do not record subsequent government compliance with it or any appeal.

Outright International's current assessment records negatives on same-sex relations, gender recognition and organisation registration without further detail, and the scope of those ratings is not elaborated in the source.
